name: Grapefruit diet

lead: The grapefruit diet is a decades-old crash diet in which dieters eat half a grapefruit, or its juice, with each meal alongside protein foods and some vegetables while avoiding sugar, grains and starchy foods. Followers use it for quick weight loss, with the appearance payoff of a leaner waist and face.

It has been popular in the United States since at least the 1930s under names such as the Hollywood diet and the 18-day diet. Proponents attribute weight loss to a fat-burning property of grapefruit, while nutrition texts and critics attribute results to the low calorie and low carbohydrate intake. Wikipedia cites no controlled trials of the plan itself.

paras: The standard version runs about 10 to 12 days followed by a short break and asks for half a grapefruit at each meal with meat, eggs and certain vegetables, and no exercise requirement. It is typically repeated in cycles by people seeking fast pre-event weight loss.

The original 18-day version reportedly provided around 500 kilocalories a day, and versions under roughly 800 to 1,000 calories are considered unhealthy. Grapefruit and its juice interact with certain medications, and it is unsuitable for people with citrus allergies. Early critics in the 1930s warned of missing nutrients.

Quick weight loss and a leaner look
angle.text: People use the plan for rapid short-term weight loss. The change in look comes from reduced calories and carbohydrates, though proponents credit grapefruit itself.

lead: The grapefruit diet, also called the Hollywood diet or the 18-day diet, is a short-term eating plan centred on eating half a grapefruit with each meal. People follow it to lose weight quickly, which is how it relates to appearance: a leaner body and less puffiness in the face and midsection. [1]

It was first described in 1929 as the eighteen-day diet and has circulated in the United States since the 1930s, with unverified rumours linking it to actress Ethel Barrymore; its originator is unknown and the Mayo Clinic has disavowed it. A 1980s revival was marketed as a ten-day plan. [1]

Proponents say grapefruit contains a fat-burning enzyme or similar substance. Nutrition literature reports no biochemical support for a fat-burning catalyst in grapefruit, and a research paper on red grapefruit looked at blood triglycerides in patients with coronary atherosclerosis rather than weight loss. [1][2][3]

paras: Dieters eat half a grapefruit at each meal together with meat, eggs and certain vegetables, and avoid sugar, most other fruit, starchy vegetables and grains, which makes the plan low in carbohydrates. The usual version lasts 10 to 12 days followed by two days off and asks for no exercise. [1]

The plan was described in 1929 and used through the 1930s; novelist Fannie Hurst is named as a follower. A 1983 article titled The grapefruit diet appeared in a trade journal, and the plan was revived in the 1980s as a ten-day plan. [1][4] Grokipedia also covers the diet and its variants. [3]
Bodybuilding forum members mention grapefruit in contest preparation discussions, but the diet appears there only in passing.
Proponents say grapefruit has fat-burning properties that speed weight loss. [1] A 1983 clinical nutrition text stated there is no biochemical support for a fat-burning catalyst effect. [1]

No studies found of the grapefruit diet itself as a weight-loss plan. Related research includes a 2006 study reporting that red grapefruit lowered serum triglycerides in patients with coronary atherosclerosis, which examined blood lipids rather than appearance. [2]

Critics in the 1930s said the diet lacked calcium, phosphorus, iron and vitamin A, and one called it dangerous. [1] Very low-calorie, very low-carbohydrate or low-micronutrient versions are described as potentially harmful, and long-term use can lead to malnutrition. [1]
Grapefruit and its juice can interact with some medicines, and grapefruit is unsuitable for people with citrus allergies; people on medication are advised to check with a clinician. [1]

timeline.event: First described as the eighteen-day diet. [1]
